o: Starting at index 0, repeatedly jump to a larger index j gaining (j − i) * nums[j]; maximize the total upon reaching the last index. Example 1: jumping straight to index 2 scores 2*8 = 16, beating the two-hop path (13). Example 2: 0→4→6 scores 4*9 + 2*3 = 42. With n ≤ 1000, O(n²) DP is fine; a monotonic stack achieves O(n).
k: dp[j] = best score to stand at j; transition dp[j] = max over i < j of dp[i] + (j − i)*nums[j].
Any hop landing on a value ≤ the value at the previous landing spot can be removed without decreasing the score, so optimal landings have strictly increasing nums values — enabling a monotonic stack.

a.i: Try every predecessor i for each j. n ≤ 1000 makes ~5*10⁵ transitions, well within limits.
s: For j from 1 to n−1: dp[j] = max(dp[i] + (j − i)*nums[j]) for i < j.

a.i: Keep a stack of indices whose nums values are strictly decreasing. When processing j, pop indices with nums ≤ nums[j] (landing on them first is never beneficial); the new top is the best predecessor, giving dp[j] = dp[top] + (j − top)*nums[j] (or j*nums[j] if the stack empties, meaning jump straight from 0).
s: For j ≥ 1: pop while nums[top] ≤ nums[j].
Let p = top if stack else 0; dp[j] = (p ? dp[p] : 0) + (j − p)*nums[j]; push j.

w: Present the DP first (simple, obviously correct), then offer the stack as optimization. Pitfall: scores can reach ~1e3 * 1e5 * hops — use 64-bit in C++/Java. Verify the stack version against Example 2 (should output 42). Follow-up: version II raises n to 1e5, requiring the O(n) stack solution.
